solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Such as Chesterton, maybe, entertaining with his stirring article

parts.note: such as is e.g., for example

indicators.note: to entertain is to hold or host, so one piece takes the others inside it

parts.note: the writer G. K. Chesterton, known by his initials; maybe marks him as one example of a GK
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer such as Chesterton is pictured amusing company with some lively piece of his.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stirring article' reads as a rousing essay, but it is a kitchen utensil for stirring.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen whisk is an article, a utensil, used to stir and beat eggs.

clue.text: Watch Italian sides being eliminated after football upset

indicators.note: in a down answer upset means turned upside down, read from the bottom
the two outer letters of the word for football are removed

parts.note: soccer is association football

explanation.surface: An Italian watch has its edges knocked off after a football fan gets upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' is not a timepiece but the imperative look!: Italian ecco means here is or behold.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian ecco is an exclamation calling attention, like look or behold.

clue.text: Get stuck into the butter!

definitions.meaning: an animal that butts with its horns

explanation.surface: An order to tuck heartily into the butter.
explanation.definitionFit: A billy or nanny of this horned animal is famous for butting, and to go at is to attack.

clue.text: Awkward when first on diet of meat sandwiches?

indicators.note: to sandwich is to hold between, so the other piece sits inside

parts.note: someone fed on a diet of ham is ham-fed
1ST, first, with the 1 written as I

explanation.surface: Someone eating only meat sandwiches is clumsy when first starting out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sandwiches' looks like food on the meat diet, but it is the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ham-fisted means clumsy or heavy-handed, as if one's hands were hams.

clue.text: What's amusing by reputation?

parts.note: a constant butt of ridicule is said to be a byword for laughter, one whose reputation makes people laugh

explanation.surface: A question about something famous for being funny.
explanation.walkthrough: A thing that is always laughed at earns that reputation; the wordplay pun is on standing as reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something long and widely ridiculed has standing, or repute, as a source of fun.

clue.text: Can pocket valuable? Hardly!

parts.note: a can is a tin
to pocket a ball in snooker is to pot it

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a can could hold a valuable, and is told no.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole phrase 'valuable? Hardly!': something far from valuable.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinpot describes something cheap, shoddy and of little worth, the opposite of valuable.

clue.text: Time to leave to pick up cold tongue?

indicators.note: to leave means the letter for time departs from the word

parts.note: to pick up on something is to sense it, to intuit it

explanation.surface: It is time to go and collect some cold tongue from the deli.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cold tongue' suggests sliced meat, but it is a language of the Arctic.
explanation.definitionFit: Inuit is the language of Arctic peoples, a tongue spoken in a cold climate.

clue.text: Banned for plagiarism in second edition

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of

indicators.note: in places the copying inside the abbreviations

parts.note: a crib is a copy, cheating by plagiarism

explanation.surface: A book is withdrawn because copied material turned up in its second edition.
explanation.definitionFit: To proscribe something is to forbid it, so proscribed means prohibited.

clue.text: Radio station's run repeated broadcast

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter widely, so the letters are scattered and rearranged
repeated means the letter for run appears twice

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A radio station's programme is run again on air.
explanation.definitionFit: A transistor is an old name for a small portable radio built with transistors.

clue.text: Seafood etc barman mostly prepared

indicators.note: food that is prepared is made ready, so these letters are reworked
mostly means all but the last letter of barman is used

explanation.surface: A barman has made most of the seafood and other bits on the bar menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the final N of BARMAN; 'prepared' rearranges ETC plus BARMA.
explanation.definitionFit: Crab meat is the flesh of crabs, eaten as a kind of seafood.

clue.text: Carbonated drink bottles finished round roof

indicators.note: to bottle is to hold in, so the drink holds the other piece inside

parts.note: cola is a fizzy soft drink
up means over or finished, as in time's up

explanation.surface: A fizzy drink company's bottles are said to be finished with a domed top.
explanation.definitionFit: A cupola is a small rounded dome forming or crowning a roof.

clue.text: Ringer that's incorporating end for our now cordless sockets

parts.note: a bell is something that rings

indicators.note: incorporating means taking into the body, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: yon is an old word for that, so that's is yon's
a butt is the end of something, such as a cigarette

explanation.surface: A doorbell push with an end fitted for sockets that no longer need a cord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cordless' suggests wireless gadgets, but it is the umbilical cord, cut at birth.
explanation.definitionFit: Navels are the hollows left where the umbilical cord was attached, now without it.

clue.text: Toy bear's in bunk

parts.note: to toy with something is to fiddle with it
bears, as in puts up with, is sticks (can't stick it)

explanation.surface: A child's teddy bear is tucked up in a bunk bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toy' and 'bear' look like nouns for a teddy, but both are verbs here; 'bunk' is nonsense, not a bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiddlesticks is an old exclamation meaning nonsense, and bunk is slang for nonsense.

clue.text: In short, "garish" is appropriate for style of French king

indicators.note: in short means a word cut short, missing its last letter

parts.note: loud means garish, gaudy
taken as written
to appropriate something is to take it, seize it

explanation.surface: A garish look suits a French king's style, briefly put.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appropriate' looks like the adjective suitable, but it is the verb take.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Seize is the decorative style of the reign of Louis XVI of France.

clue.text: King and I set makes for cracking musical

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: cracking means breaking up, so the letters are broken and reformed

explanation.surface: The King and I is set up to become a cracking musical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King and I' recalls a different musical, The King and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Kiss Me, Kate is Cole Porter's Broadway show based on The Taming of the Shrew.

clue.text: He passed on book two in series of books

indicators.note: in places the book and the numeral inside the series of books

parts.note: OT is the Old Testament, a series of books of the Bible
II is two in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A man handed on the second volume in a set of books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'passed on' suggests handing something over, but it means died: OBIIT is Latin for 'he (or she) died', seen on tombstones.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin verb, abbreviated ob. on memorials, records that a person died.

clue.text: Cancels course if ill, unable to return displays

indicators.note: to return says the hidden letters are read backwards
displays says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone drops out of a course because, being ill, they cannot come back.
explanation.definitionFit: To nullify something is to make it void, which is to cancel it.

clue.text: Move inch by inch?

parts.note: inch is a Scottish word for a small island, so moving from one inch to the next is touring islands

explanation.surface: A question about creeping along very slowly.
explanation.walkthrough: An inch is Scottish for a small island, as in Inchcolm; moving inch by inch is travelling island to island.
explanation.definitionFit: To island-hop is to travel from one island to another in turn.

clue.text: Jailed by judge, ex-pupil's assisted crime

parts.note: someone in prison is inside
OB, old boy, is a former pupil of a school

explanation.surface: A former schoolboy is sent to prison by a judge for helping in a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: An inside job is a crime committed with help from someone within the targeted organisation.

clue.text: Stop at sea to tell some tales?

definitions.meaning: a ship lies to when it comes nearly to a halt, head to the wind
telling tales to someone is telling them falsehoods

explanation.surface: A sailor halts the ship to spin a few yarns.
explanation.definitionFit: The nautical phrase means to heave to and stop; the everyday phrase means to deceive someone.

clue.text: Designates perimeter of park especially for winter sport

indicators.note: read as e-specially, the letters are made up in a special way, rearranged
the perimeter is the outer edge, so the first and last letters of park

explanation.surface: Someone marks off the edge of a park specially for a winter game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'especially' is the anagram signal: DESIGNATES plus PK are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Speed skating is racing on ice skates, an event at the Winter Olympics.

clue.text: Band ultimately mean to raise flag

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the last letter of band
in a down answer to raise means read upwards, reversed

parts.note: poor means mean, of low quality

explanation.surface: A band finally means to hoist a flag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flag' looks like a banner to hoist, but it is the verb tire.
explanation.definitionFit: To flag is to tire and sag, which is to droop.

clue.text: What's oddly featured by satellite state

parts.note: Io is a moon of Jupiter

indicators.note: oddly means the odd-numbered letters, first and third

explanation.surface: A question about what odd thing a satellite has picked up in some state.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as is, a link: the odd letters of WHAT follow IO.
explanation.definitionFit: Iowa is a state in the American Midwest.

clue.text: Approach of mine having commercial appeal

parts.note: an ad is a commercial
it means sex appeal, as in the it girl

explanation.surface: Someone's way of working has a marketable charm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Approach of mine' reads as my method, but it is an entrance to a mine.
explanation.definitionFit: An adit is a horizontal passage giving access into a mine.

clue.text: Running without queen's backing

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: W/O is a common written abbreviation for without
a rani is an Indian queen

explanation.surface: A race is run without the queen supporting it.
explanation.definitionFit: Things happening in a row happen one after another, consecutively, as in three days running.

clue.text: Cried several times over, with husband involved in plot

indicators.note: in places the run of letters inside the plot

parts.note: a plot of ground in a garden is a bed

indicators.note: involved means taken inside, so the husband sits among the overs

parts.note: O stands for over in cricket, so several overs give a run of Os

explanation.surface: Someone wept again and again on finding their husband was in on a scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: The Os are 'several times over': four overs, with H set in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Boo-hoo imitates loud sobbing, so to have boohooed is to have wept noisily.

clue.text: Partner of old politician getting into film for free

parts.note: an ex is a former partner

indicators.note: getting into means entering, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: ET is Spielberg's film E.T.
MP, member of parliament, is a politician

explanation.surface: A former partner of a politician from the past lands a part in a film without paying.
explanation.definitionFit: Being exempt means being excused from an obligation, so free of it.

clue.text: Biased when accepting Houses of Parliament as constitutional asset?

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: aslant means slanting, at an angle, biased

explanation.surface: Someone is accused of bias for treating Parliament as a constitutional asset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'constitutional' suggests government, but a constitutional is a health-giving walk; the asset is a walking stick made of ash wood.
explanation.definitionFit: An ash plant is a walking stick cut from an ash sapling, useful on a stroll.
